cases.ruling: Taking an additional step, tucking the ball and turning upfield, extending the ball, or avoiding an opponent
cases.explanation: According to the NFL rule on completing a catch, after a player has control of a forward pass, a football act is defined as any action common to the game or maintaining control long enough to perform one. cases.question: When does losing the ball while going to the ground make a pass incomplete?
cases.ruling: The pass is incomplete when a player who has control and has gotten two feet (or another qualifying body part) down loses control upon contacting the ground before performing a football act or maintaining control long enough to perform one.
cases.explanation: According to the rule, if a player has control and has two feet (or another qualifying body part) down but has not yet performed a football act or maintained control long enough to perform one, then losing control when contacting the ground makes the pass incomplete. The player does not need to keep control through the ground after all elements of the catch were already completed; a later loss can instead be a fumble. The ball may touch the ground without forcing an incompletion when the player maintains control and the ground does not cause the loss of control.

cases.question: Is a pass automatically incomplete whenever the ball touches the ground?
cases.ruling: No, a pass is not automatically incomplete whenever the ball touches the ground; it depends on whether the player had control and whether control was lost before completing the catch.
cases.explanation: The rules state that a forward pass must be controlled before it touches the ground, and the player must then touch the ground inbounds with both feet or another qualifying body part and perform a football act or maintain control long enough to perform one. If the ball touches the ground after the player has control but before completing the catch, the pass is incomplete only if control is lost when contacting the ground. The ball may touch the ground without forcing an incompletion if the player maintains control and the ground does not cause the loss of control. Therefore, a ball touching the ground does not automatically make the pass incomplete; it is contingent on control and the completion criteria.

cases.explanation: According to the rule, a defensive penalty can produce a new series by moving the ball to the line to gain or by awarding an automatic first down. This means that if a defensive penalty is accepted, the offense receives a new set of downs.

cases.question: What conditions make a forward pass legal?
cases.ruling: A forward pass is legal when it is the offense’s first forward pass of the down, the ball is released from behind the line of scrimmage, the passer’s entire body and the ball are not beyond the line at the moment of release, and the pass is not made after a change of possession. The pass must also be initiated by an intentional forward movement of the passer’s hand.
cases.explanation: The rules state that the offense may throw one forward pass during a down and that the pass must be released from behind the line of scrimmage (chunk 0f214c9be67378d7). A pass is illegal if it is a second forward pass, is released after a change of possession, or is released when the passer’s entire body and the ball are beyond the line of scrimmage (chunk 0f214c9be67378d7). Additionally, a forward pass begins with an intentional forward movement of the passer’s hand (chunk f863dc681ed93e5b). Therefore, a forward pass is legal only when it satisfies all of these conditions.

cases.question: How can a passer outside the pocket avoid intentional grounding?
cases.ruling: Throw the ball to or beyond the line of scrimmage.
cases.explanation: According to the rule, a passer who has been outside the pocket avoids intentional grounding by throwing the ball to or beyond the line of scrimmage, even if no receiver has a realistic chance to catch it. This satisfies the requirement that the pass be to a realistic eligible receiver or beyond the line of scrimmage to avoid grounding.

cases.question: Which offensive positions are eligible receivers?
cases.ruling: Eligible receivers are the players on the two ends of the line of scrimmage and any players positioned at least one yard behind the line; interior linemen between the ends are not eligible. Eligible receivers must wear eligible numbers or have reported eligible status.
cases.explanation: The rules state that for a forward pass from behind the line of scrimmage, the eligible offensive receivers are the players on the two ends of the line and those positioned at least one yard behind the line. Interior linemen between the two ends are not eligible receivers merely because they wear an eligible number. Eligible receivers must wear eligible numbers or have reported an eligible status when the rules permit reporting.

cases.question: He secures the pass, taps both toes inbounds, turns upfield, and only then loses the ball. Was the reception already completed?
cases.ruling: Yes, the reception was already completed.
cases.explanation: The player first secured control of the ball, then tapped both toes inbounds, and performed a football act by turning upfield. According to the rules, once a player has control, establishes both feet inbounds, and performs a football act (or maintains control long enough to perform one), the catch is complete. A later loss of control after that act is treated as a fumble, not an incomplete pass. Therefore the reception was completed before the ball was lost.

cases.question: For a receiver at the goal line, how do the completed-catch requirements and the touchdown rule work together?
cases.ruling: The receiver must first complete the catch before the ball is considered possessed on the goal line and a touchdown is scored.
cases.explanation: A receiver at the goal line must satisfy the catch requirements—control before the ball touches the ground, two in‑bounds feet (or another qualifying body part), and a football act or sufficient control—before the ball is considered possessed on the goal line. Only after the catch is completed can the ball be possessed on, above, or beyond the goal‑line plane, which satisfies the touchdown requirement. The ball becomes dead immediately when the touchdown requirement is met.
